```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE, comment="#>", fig.width=7.2,
                    fig.height=4.5, dpi=120)
library(geosmooth)
```

PCA describes directions with large variation in the predictors. PLS also uses
the training response, so it can retain a direction with little geometric
variation but a strong relationship with the response. This advantage is
conditional: a noisy binary response can give unstable supervised directions,
and neither method guarantees that a small chart captures a nonlinear response.

This vignette compares the methods using known binary-response probabilities.
It separates two questions: does unfolding remove a geometric bend, and does a
response-informed chart improve prediction? All computations below use the
public `fit.local.likelihood()` and `unfold.simplex.chart()` interfaces.
The [local simplex charts guide](local-simplex-charts.html) gives the mathematical
and implementation details.

## First inspect the geometry

We place points on two adjacent faces of the nonnegative max-normalized simplex.
A latent coordinate `t` runs from -0.2 to 0.2. It maps to `(1, 1+t)` on one face
and `(1-t, 1)` on the other. Additional coordinates vary below one. The simplex
is the surface with at least one coordinate equal to one; distances are shortest
Euclidean-length paths constrained to that surface.

```{r seam-geometry, fig.cap="A straight latent coordinate appears bent in ambient coordinates. Unfolding rotates the adjacent face into the query face; both axes use the same physical scale.", fig.alt="Two panels show a right-angle seam before unfolding and a straight line afterward."}
t.line <- c(seq(-.2, -.005, length.out=30), seq(.005, .2, length.out=30))
seam <- cbind(ifelse(t.line < 0, 1, 1-t.line),
              ifelse(t.line < 0, 1+t.line, 1), .2)
flat <- unfold.simplex.chart(seam, c(1, .95, .2))
stopifnot(flat$certified)
old.par <- par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(4,4,2,1))
plot(seam[,1:2], asp=1, pch=16, col="#0072B2", xlim=c(.76,1.24),
     ylim=c(.76,1.24), xlab="First coordinate", ylab="Second coordinate",
     main="Ambient coordinates")
plot(flat$coordinates[,1:2], asp=1, pch=16, col="#009E73",
     xlim=c(.76,1.24), ylim=c(.76,1.24), xlab="First coordinate",
     ylab="Unfolded second coordinate", main="Unfolded coordinates")
par(old.par)
variance.one <- function(x) {
    values <- svd(scale(x, center=TRUE, scale=FALSE), nu=0, nv=0)$d^2
    values[1]/sum(values)
}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Chart=c("Ambient", "Unfolded"),
    `Variance retained by one PC (%)`=100*c(variance.one(seam),
        variance.one(flat$coordinates)), check.names=FALSE), digits=1)
```

Retaining more variance is a geometric result, not evidence of better outcome
prediction. The examples below test prediction separately. Both folded and
unfolded charts use the same intrinsic neighbors and weights. Unfolding can be
rejected near corners, tied maxima or more than two faces; such cases are counted
rather than silently forced into a chart.

## Define examples before comparing methods

Each observation has six coordinates. The seam coordinate `t` and a broad
coordinate `u3` vary substantially. A narrow coordinate `u4` has a much smaller
range; the remaining two coordinates are nuisance features. The table gives the
true log odds. The true probability is `plogis(eta)` and the observed response is
a Bernoulli draw with that probability.

| Example | True log odds, eta | Question |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Seam | -1 + 2 t/0.2 | Does a chart retain variation across the bend? |
| High variance | -1 + 2 (u3-0.3)/0.2 | Can PCA capture a signal aligned with broad variation? |
| Low variance | -1 + 2 (u4-0.12)/0.02 | Does supervised PLS recover a narrow signal direction? |
| Constant | -1 | Does adaptation to binary noise hurt prediction? |
| Nonlinear | -1 + 2.5 ((t/0.2)^2 - 1/3) | How do local linear charts handle a symmetric nonlinear signal? |

The narrow coordinate varies from 0.10 to 0.14. Its contribution to the log odds
is deliberately as large as that of the broad coordinate in the high-variance
example. This is a stress test for variance-based dimension reduction, not a
claim about the frequency of such signals in real datasets. Predictor features
are not standardized before constructing directions: doing so would change the
geometry and would remove part of the contrast we intend to study. Component
scores are scaled inside the local logistic fit.

```{r generator}
scenarios <- c("Seam", "High variance", "Low variance", "Constant", "Nonlinear")
make.example <- function(seed, scenario, n=360L) {
    set.seed(seed)
    t <- runif(n, -.2, .2)
    X <- cbind(ifelse(t < 0, 1, 1-t), ifelse(t < 0, 1+t, 1),
               runif(n, .1, .5), runif(n, .10, .14),
               runif(n, .02, .06), runif(n, .02, .06))
    eta <- switch(scenario,
        "Seam"=-1+2*t/.2,
        "High variance"=-1+2*(X[,3]-.3)/.2,
        "Low variance"=-1+2*(X[,4]-.12)/.02,
        "Constant"=rep(-1,n),
        "Nonlinear"=-1+2.5*((t/.2)^2-1/3))
    probability <- plogis(eta)
    list(X=X, y=rbinom(n,1,probability), probability=probability, t=t)
}
```

## Fit on training observations; choose dimension on tuning observations

Each of five independent repetitions per example has **180 training**, **60
tuning** and **120 test** observations. The observations are independent in this
simulation. For repeated specimens or matched sets, splitting must respect those
groups instead.

We compare ambient PCA, unfolded PCA and unfolded PLS. All use 60 training
neighbors, Gaussian weights, a fixed slope ridge penalty of 1, and half-success/
half-failure intercept pseudo-counts. Support size and ridge penalty are held
fixed to make the chart comparison interpretable; they are not claimed optimal.

We report both a fixed one-dimensional chart and a chart dimension chosen from
1, 2 and 3 by the lowest tuning Brier loss. Ties choose the first (smaller)
dimension. Tuning predictions use training observations only. Final test
predictions use the same training fits; the tuning observations are not added to
the training set. Test outcomes and true probabilities never select the model.

```{r fit-helper}
methods <- c("Ambient PCA", "Unfolded PCA", "Unfolded PLS")
fit.chart <- function(X, y, query, method, dimension, degree=1L) {
    fit.local.likelihood(X, y, X.eval=query, likelihood.family="bernoulli",
        chart.geometry="linf.simplex", unfold.faces=method != "Ambient PCA",
        coordinate.method=if (method == "Unfolded PLS") "local.pls" else "local.pca",
        support.size=60L, chart.dim=dimension, degree=degree,
        kernel="gaussian", lambda.ridge=1, intercept.mass=.5,
        max.iter=70L, tol=1e-7, fallback="degree0")
}
train <- 1:180
tune <- 181:240
test <- 241:360
```

Here is a complete fit for the low-variance example. Replacing `"Unfolded PLS"`
with `"Unfolded PCA"` changes the directions while retaining the same geometry
and likelihood settings.

```{r single-fit, eval=FALSE}
dat <- make.example(271301, "Low variance")
fit <- fit.chart(dat$X[train,], dat$y[train], dat$X[test,],
                 "Unfolded PLS", dimension=1L)
head(fit$fitted.values)
fit$diagnostics$status.counts
```

The following loop executes the comparison. A local constant uses the same
neighbors and weights but no chart directions. A global constant uses the
smoothed overall training proportion. Both are useful controls, particularly
when the true probability is constant.

```{r comparison}
rows <- list()
illustrations <- list()
append.result <- function(scenario, repetition, method, mode, dimension,
                          prediction, truth, response, fallbacks, tuning.fallbacks=NA_integer_) {
    stopifnot(all(is.finite(prediction)), all(prediction > 0 & prediction < 1))
    data.frame(scenario=scenario, repetition=repetition, method=method,
        mode=mode, dimension=dimension,
        probability.mse=mean((prediction-truth)^2),
        brier=mean((prediction-response)^2),
        log.loss=-mean(response*log(prediction)+(1-response)*log1p(-prediction)),
        fallbacks=fallbacks, tuning.fallbacks=tuning.fallbacks)
}
for (s in seq_along(scenarios)) for (repetition in 1:5) {
    scenario <- scenarios[s]
    dat <- make.example(271000+100*s+repetition, scenario)
    example.predictions <- list()
    for (method in methods) {
        fits <- lapply(1:3, function(d) fit.chart(dat$X[train,], dat$y[train],
            dat$X[c(tune,test),], method, d))
        tuning.loss <- vapply(fits, function(f)
            mean((f$fitted.values[1:60]-dat$y[tune])^2), numeric(1))
        best <- which.min(tuning.loss)
        for (mode in c("One dimension", "Tuned dimension")) {
            d <- if (mode == "One dimension") 1L else best
            chosen <- fits[[d]]
            prediction <- chosen$fitted.values[61:180]
            rows[[length(rows)+1L]] <- append.result(scenario, repetition, method,
                mode, d, prediction, dat$probability[test], dat$y[test],
                sum(chosen$diagnostics$per.eval$fallback[61:180]),
                sum(chosen$diagnostics$per.eval$fallback[1:60]))
            if (repetition == 1L) example.predictions[[paste(method,mode)]] <- prediction
        }
    }
    local <- fit.chart(dat$X[train,], dat$y[train], dat$X[test,],
                       "Ambient PCA", dimension=1L, degree=0L)
    constants <- list("Local constant"=local$fitted.values,
        "Global constant"=rep((sum(dat$y[train])+.5)/(length(train)+1), length(test)))
    for (method in names(constants)) {
        rows[[length(rows)+1L]] <- append.result(scenario, repetition, method,
            "Constant", 0L, constants[[method]], dat$probability[test], dat$y[test], 0L)
        if (repetition == 1L) example.predictions[[method]] <- constants[[method]]
    }
    if (repetition == 1L) illustrations[[scenario]] <- list(data=dat,
        predictions=example.predictions)
}
results <- do.call(rbind, rows)
stopifnot(nrow(results) == 200L)
```

## Measure estimation and prediction separately

**Probability mean squared error (MSE)** compares the predicted probability with
the known true probability. It directly measures estimation accuracy here.
**Brier loss** compares the prediction with the binary response; it includes
irreducible Bernoulli variation. Lower values are better for both. Test log loss
is also retained in `results` for inspection. Neither a low MSE nor a converged
optimizer alone establishes uncertainty calibration.

The table shows the mean across five repetitions. The figures show every
repetition as well as the mean, so an apparently favorable average cannot hide a
reversal. Five repetitions make a compact teaching example, not a powered
simulation study or a universal ranking of methods.

```{r performance-table}
summary.table <- aggregate(cbind(probability.mse,brier) ~ scenario+method+mode,
                           results, mean)
summary.table <- summary.table[order(match(summary.table$scenario, scenarios),
    match(summary.table$mode,c("One dimension","Tuned dimension","Constant")),
    match(summary.table$method,c(methods,"Local constant","Global constant"))),]
knitr::kable(summary.table, digits=4, row.names=FALSE,
    col.names=c("Example","Method","Chart","Probability MSE","Brier loss"))
```

```{r performance-figure, fig.height=8, fig.cap="Held-out probability error for all five repetitions. Small points are independent repetitions; diamonds are their means. Each panel uses its own labelled vertical scale. Lower is better. The constant baselines are identical in the two columns.", fig.alt="Ten panels compare probability mean squared error across methods, with all repetitions and means shown for fixed and tuned chart dimensions."}
colors <- c("Ambient PCA"="#0072B2", "Unfolded PCA"="#009E73",
    "Unfolded PLS"="#D55E00", "Local constant"="#666666", "Global constant"="#AA4499")
labels <- c("PCA", "Unfolded\nPCA", "Unfolded\nPLS", "Local\nconstant", "Global\nconstant")
old.par <- par(mfrow=c(5,2), mar=c(3.2,4,2,1), oma=c(0,0,1,0), cex=.8)
for (scenario in scenarios) for (mode in c("One dimension","Tuned dimension")) {
    tab <- results[results$scenario==scenario & results$mode %in% c(mode,"Constant"),]
    order.methods <- names(colors)
    plot(NA, xlim=c(.7,5.3), ylim=c(0, max(tab$probability.mse)*1.08+1e-6),
         xaxt="n", xlab="", ylab="Probability MSE", main=paste(scenario,mode,sep=" — "))
    axis(1, at=1:5, labels=labels, cex.axis=.8)
    for (j in 1:5) {
        values <- tab$probability.mse[tab$method==order.methods[j]]
        points(j+seq(-.12,.12,length.out=5), values, pch=16, cex=.7,
               col=adjustcolor(colors[j],alpha.f=.6))
        points(j, mean(values), pch=18, cex=1.3, col=colors[j])
    }
}
par(old.par)
```

## Inspect the first repetition, without choosing favorable seeds

The following plot compares predicted and true probabilities on the independent
test observations from the **first predeclared repetition** of each example.
Each point is one test observation. The diagonal is exact probability recovery,
not a fitted regression line. Constant-probability observations share the same
horizontal coordinate; vertical spread there shows adaptation to noise.

```{r predictions-figure, fig.height=8, fig.cap="Predicted versus known true probabilities for first-repetition test observations. Columns compare unfolded PCA and PLS, each with one dimension. Points near the diagonal recover the true probabilities; all panels share the same axes.", fig.alt="Ten scatterplots show true versus predicted test probabilities for unfolded PCA and unfolded PLS, including constant and nonlinear cases."}
old.par <- par(mfrow=c(5,2), mar=c(3,3.3,2,1), cex=.8)
for (scenario in scenarios) for (method in c("Unfolded PCA","Unfolded PLS")) {
    item <- illustrations[[scenario]]
    prediction <- item$predictions[[paste(method,"One dimension")]]
    plot(item$data$probability[test], prediction, xlim=c(0,1), ylim=c(0,1),
         xlab="True probability", ylab="Predicted probability", pch=16, cex=.65,
         col=adjustcolor(colors[method],alpha.f=.55), main=paste(scenario,method,sep=" — "))
    abline(0,1,lty=2,col="grey35")
}
par(old.par)
```

## View the estimated probability functions

These slices use the first repetition's training observations. The signal
coordinate varies over its generating range while nuisance coordinates are
held at the centers of their ranges. They show the fitted conditional function
at defined locations, not averages of the scatterplots above. The black curve
is the known truth. All methods use one-dimensional charts; they are not
retuned on the displayed slices.

```{r slice-figure, fig.height=7.5, fig.cap="Conditional probability slices through the same first-repetition training fits. Nuisance coordinates are fixed at their generating centers. Black is the known truth; colored curves use one-dimensional charts. All probability axes run from zero to one.", fig.alt="Five probability curves compare the known truth with ambient PCA, unfolded PCA and unfolded PLS as the signal coordinate changes."}
slices <- list()
old.par <- par(mfrow=c(3,2), mar=c(4,4,2,1), cex=.85)
for (scenario in scenarios) {
    grid <- seq(-1,1,length.out=60)
    t <- if (scenario %in% c("Seam","Nonlinear","Constant")) .2*grid else rep(.08,60)
    X.slice <- cbind(ifelse(t < 0,1,1-t), ifelse(t < 0,1+t,1), .3,.12,.04,.04)
    if (scenario=="High variance") X.slice[,3] <- .3+.2*grid
    if (scenario=="Low variance") X.slice[,4] <- .12+.02*grid
    eta <- if (scenario=="Constant") rep(-1,60) else if (scenario=="Nonlinear")
        -1+2.5*(grid^2-1/3) else -1+2*grid
    truth <- plogis(eta)
    dat <- illustrations[[scenario]]$data
    prediction <- vapply(methods, function(method)
        fit.chart(dat$X[train,],dat$y[train],X.slice,method,1L)$fitted.values,
        numeric(60))
    axis.value <- if (scenario=="High variance") X.slice[,3] else if (scenario=="Low variance")
        X.slice[,4] else t
    axis.label <- if (scenario=="High variance") "Broad coordinate u3" else if (scenario=="Low variance")
        "Narrow coordinate u4" else "Seam coordinate t"
    plot(axis.value,truth,type="l",lwd=2,col="black",ylim=c(0,1),
         xlab=axis.label,ylab="Probability",main=scenario)
    for (j in seq_along(methods)) lines(axis.value,prediction[,j],col=colors[j],lwd=1.5,lty=j)
    slices[[scenario]] <- list(X=X.slice,truth=truth,prediction=prediction)
}
plot.new()
legend("center",c("Truth",methods),col=c("black",colors[methods]),
       lty=c(1,1,2,3),lwd=c(2,1.5,1.5,1.5),bty="n",cex=.9)
par(old.par)
```

## Check selected dimensions and fallbacks

```{r diagnostic-tables}
tuned <- results[results$mode=="Tuned dimension",]
selection <- as.data.frame(xtabs(~scenario+method+dimension, tuned))
selection <- selection[selection$Freq>0,]
knitr::kable(selection, row.names=FALSE,
    col.names=c("Example","Method","Selected dimension","Repetitions"))
knitr::kable(aggregate(cbind(fallbacks,tuning.fallbacks) ~ scenario+method+mode,
                      results, sum), row.names=FALSE,
    col.names=c("Example","Method","Chart","Test fallbacks","Tuning fallbacks"))
```

A fallback is a failed chart certificate or failed optimizer replaced by the
smoothed local proportion. Such predictions remain in the performance scores.
They are not discarded to improve apparent performance. The table counts only
reported rank-one or selected fits; its two modes reuse some fits and must not
be added together as independent failures. `results` also retains each selected
dimension and each test log loss.

## Reading the comparison

The low-variance example shows why response-informed directions are not enough
by themselves. With one dimension, unfolded PCA and PLS have mean probability
MSEs of `r sprintf("%.4f", subset(summary.table, scenario=="Low variance" & method=="Unfolded PCA" & mode=="One dimension")$probability.mse)` and
`r sprintf("%.4f", subset(summary.table, scenario=="Low variance" & method=="Unfolded PLS" & mode=="One dimension")$probability.mse)`, respectively.
After selecting dimension on the tuning observations, these become
`r sprintf("%.4f", subset(summary.table, scenario=="Low variance" & method=="Unfolded PCA" & mode=="Tuned dimension")$probability.mse)` and
`r sprintf("%.4f", subset(summary.table, scenario=="Low variance" & method=="Unfolded PLS" & mode=="Tuned dimension")$probability.mse)`.
Weighted PLS uses covariance and is still affected by predictor scale, binary
noise and the number of retained directions. Its narrow-signal advantage here
appears after dimension selection, not from its first direction alone.

The constant example favors the global constant in known-probability MSE. In
the high-variance example, dimension-tuned PCA has a smaller mean probability
MSE than dimension-tuned PLS. Dimension tuning itself sometimes worsens test
performance relative to the one-dimensional fit: 60 tuning observations give
a noisy selection criterion. These comparisons explain why the vignette shows
baselines, fixed and selected dimensions, and every repetition.

The seam example distinguishes correcting a geometric fold from learning a
response direction. The high-variance example is favorable to PCA's criterion;
the low-variance example deliberately puts important response information in a
direction PCA may discard. Increasing the chart dimension gives PCA a chance to
recover that information, with additional estimation variability. PLS can help
at low dimension, but its supervised directions must be learned exclusively
from training data.

The constant example is an essential control: there is no informative direction
to recover. The nonlinear example asks whether local neighborhoods make a
nonlinear function adequately linear; the local PLS covariance can be weak near
symmetry points even when the response depends strongly on position. No method
is assumed to win these comparisons. Differences among individual repetitions,
not just averages, matter.

For a scientific analysis, expand the simulation to realistic sample sizes,
class balance, dependence, missingness and geometry. Tune support size and
regularization inside training data, assess probability calibration on an outer
hold-out sample, and examine performance near corners or low-support regions.
For case-control sampling, recovering conditional probability in the selected
sample does not identify population prevalence without sampling information.

## Reproduce and adapt

All results and figures are computed by this vignette. No cohort data, saved
outcome fits or Python reference predictions are read. The 25 seeds and all
settings are fixed in the code. The workload is serial; it can be rendered with
single-threaded BLAS/OpenMP to avoid competing with other analyses. See
`?fit.local.likelihood` and `?unfold.simplex.chart` for controls and diagnostics.

```{r save-validation, include=FALSE}
# A developer may request a machine-readable audit copy; ordinary vignette
# builds do not write outside knitr's output directory.
audit.path <- Sys.getenv("GEOSMOOTH_VIGNETTE_AUDIT", unset="")
if (nzchar(audit.path)) saveRDS(list(results=results, illustrations=illustrations,
    slices=slices, summary=summary.table, session=sessionInfo()), audit.path)
```

```{r session, echo=FALSE}
packageVersion("geosmooth")
packageVersion("dgraphs")
```
